title: How HTTPS Keeps Your Data Private

audience.knows: they use browsers and see a padlock, little about how it works
audience.cares_about: whether what they type at work and at home can be read by anyone else

outcome: After watching, the viewer can explain in their own words why a padlocked site protects what they send, and can say what to check before typing something sensitive
through_line: The padlock is not decoration: it is the result of a quick check and a shared secret, so a message crossing the open network is useless to anyone but its two ends

arc_plan.what: A login or payment form is submitted and the data crosses a crowded network in plain sight; a watcher in the middle reads it. The viewer recognises the everyday moment and feels the exposure
Promise the viewer will follow one request from browser to server and be able to say why the watcher now sees only noise, and what the padlock does and does not tell them
Optional link from the exposed message to the idea of locking it
arc_plan.needs: Not needed for a two minute lesson; the promise leads straight into the build

arc_plan.what: One running request, shown as a system in motion. Section one: the browser asks the server to identify itself and checks its certificate. Section two: the two sides agree a shared key without sending it in the open. Section three: data is scrambled with that key, travels as noise past the watcher and is unscrambled at the far end
The viewer is shown a new situation, for example a site whose certificate check fails, and chooses what the browser should do and why, so they can pass it from what they just saw
A short habit for the viewer: what to look at before entering sensitive data, and the limit of what the padlock proves
Return to the opening form: same data, same network, same watcher, now seeing only scrambled noise, and the padlock closing

must_cover.what: Why plain traffic can be read by anyone on the path
The server proves its identity with a certificate that the browser checks
Browser and server agree a shared key without exposing it to the watcher
Data is encrypted with that key and decrypted at the other end, so interceptors see only scrambled data
What the padlock means and what it does not guarantee

must_avoid: Opening with a glossary-style explanation or an agenda
Any statistic or figure without a source
Jargon before the picture that explains it
Drawing the encryption maths in depth
Fear-mongering or talking down to the viewer
Claiming the padlock means a site is trustworthy
example_posture: One running example throughout: a single form submission from a browser to a server with one watcher on the path. Reuse it in hook, build, check and payoff; no separate examples. Use plain generic names, no real brands.
visual_direction: Pure motion graphics on the plain light corporate field. Mostly the system in motion: a browser and a server, data travelling between them as packets, a certificate being inspected, two keys coming together, readable data visibly turning into scrambled data and back, a padlock closing. Crisp shapes, clear labels, one loud thing at a time, purposeful motion, one board that changes by additions. No people, no textures, no sets.
voice_note: Analyst persona: precise, calm, a colleague walking through a diagram. Name each idea only after it has been seen on screen.
open_questions: Which facts the knowledge sheet will fix about the key agreement step, kept at a level suited to non-specialists
Whether the check should use a failed certificate or another scenario

inferred: running example of a form submission with a watcher

look.note: Pure motion graphics on a clean corporate background, mostly the system itself in motion; technical but clean and beautiful
